1.text:
Leftovers From Building the Planets

When the planets formed, not every scrap of rock and ice got used. Some leftovers are still out there today, zipping around the Sun. This deck is all about those small bodies, and it starts with a big question: can they hit us?

Here's the road map. First come asteroids, the rocky leftovers about 4.6 billion years old, most of them in a belt between Mars and Jupiter. Then comets, the icy leftovers that grow glowing heads and tails near the Sun. After that we visit the two places comets come from, the Kuiper Belt and the Oort Cloud, and find out why Pluto, Ceres and Eris are called dwarf planets. We finish with space rocks that actually reach Earth: meteors, meteorites and craters, from Arizona to the death of the dinosaurs, plus the day NASA pushed an asteroid on purpose.

Before you start, jot down a quick answer: what's the difference between an asteroid, a comet and a meteor? Hang on to it. Most people mix the three up, and you'll check yourself at the end.

Did you know? Pluto didn't shrink or move in 2006. What changed was the definition of the word "planet."

2.text:
Today I Can...

Here's what you'll be able to do by the end of this deck. Copy these into your notebook as "I can" statements and rate yourself 1 to 3 on each one now.

I can describe the asteroid belt and why Jupiter kept a planet from forming there. I can compare C-, S- and M-type asteroids and explain their small total mass. I can label a comet's nucleus, coma and two tails, and say where the tails point. I can describe the Kuiper Belt and Oort Cloud as the homes of comets. I can use Kepler's third law to find a comet's orbital period. I can use the IAU rules to explain why Pluto, Ceres and Eris are dwarf planets.

I can also tell a meteoroid, a meteor and a meteorite apart and explain meteor showers. I can explain how near-Earth objects are tracked and how DART changed an orbit. And I can explain Meteor Crater, Chicxulub, and why Earth shows fewer craters than the Moon. A few of these are "enrichment" goals, which means they aren't named in the Indiana standards, but they're part of this course and they set up the Earth decks coming next quarter. So yes, they count!

3.text:
The Asteroid Belt

An asteroid is a small rocky body orbiting the Sun, left over from building the planets. Asteroids are sometimes called minor planets. Most of them orbit between Mars and Jupiter in the main asteroid belt, and Jupiter's gravity rules the neighborhood.

How many are there? The belt holds an estimated 1.1 to 1.9 million asteroids larger than 1 km, plus millions of smaller ones. They range from Ceres, about 940 km across and now called a dwarf planet, and Vesta, the largest true asteroid at about 530 km across, down to rocks less than 10 m wide. Most are lumpy, pitted and cratered, not round, and more than 150 are known to have their own small moons.

Not every asteroid lives in the belt. The Jupiter trojans share Jupiter's orbit, gathered at two spots 60 degrees ahead of and behind the planet, and there may be about as many of them as there are belt asteroids. Near-Earth asteroids have orbits that come close to ours. As the slide says, the picture is not to scale.

Did you know? As of April 2026, the Minor Planet Center, the worldwide clearing house for these objects, listed 1,447,896 main-belt asteroids and 16,730 Jupiter trojans with known orbits.

4.text:
Why No Planet Formed Here

So why is there a belt of rubble instead of a fifth rocky planet? Blame Jupiter. Early in the solar system's history, the gravity of newly formed Jupiter stirred up this region. The small bodies crashed into each other and broke apart instead of sticking together. No planet ever formed here, and none exploded either. NASA calls Ceres an "embryonic planet" that started to grow but never finished.

Jupiter still shapes the belt today. Look at the graph of asteroid counts against distance from the Sun, from 2.0 to 3.5 AU. Notice the empty lanes. Those are Kirkwood gaps: lanes in the belt that Jupiter's repeated tugs keep nearly empty. The gap labeled 3:1 is where an asteroid would make 3 laps around the Sun for every 1 lap Jupiter makes. That asteroid gets the same tug at the same spot again and again, and the tugs add up until it's pulled out of that lane.

You can find the gaps with Kepler's third law. Jupiter takes 11.86 years to orbit, so an asteroid in the 3:1 lane would take 11.86 / 3 = 3.95 years. Plug that into P2 = a3 and you get about 2.5 AU, right where the 3:1 gap sits. The other gaps land at about 2.83 AU (5:2), 2.96 AU (7:3) and 3.28 AU (2:1). The bars on this slide are only a sketch of the shape, not real data.

Did you know? Jupiter's tugs can push asteroids out of the belt entirely and across the paths of other planets. That's one way near-Earth asteroids are made.

5.text:
What Asteroids Are Made Of

Asteroids aren't all the same gray rock. NASA sorts them into three broad types. C-type, or "chondrite," asteroids are the most common: dark clay and silicate rock, among the oldest objects in the solar system. S-type, or "stony," asteroids are silicate rock mixed with nickel-iron. M-type asteroids are metallic, mostly nickel-iron metal.

Why the differences? It depends on how far from the Sun each asteroid formed. Some young asteroids also got hot and partly melted. Iron sank to the center and lava was pushed to the surface, the same layering that gave Earth its iron core. Break one of those apart and you get chunks of pure metal. No aliens required.

We even have samples. More than 50,000 meteorites have been found, and 99.8% of them come from asteroids. Some have been traced to Vesta by NASA's Dawn mission. NASA's OSIRIS-REx went further: it grabbed rock and dust from the asteroid Bennu in October 2020 and dropped the sample capsule in Utah on 24 September 2023.

Did you know? C-type asteroids are dark because of their carbon-rich clay, not because they got burned.

6.text:
The Whole Belt Is Lightweight

More than a million asteroids sounds like a lot of stuff. But add up every asteroid in the belt, and the total mass is still less than our Moon's. The Moon still wins!

One body hogs the scale. About a third of the belt's mass is in Ceres, the big one. Estimates vary: NASA's Ceres page says 25%, and another calculation puts it nearer 39%, so "about a third" is the safe way to say it. Even Ceres is tiny next to Pluto, which is 14 times more massive.

Why so little? Early Jupiter stirred the region so the pieces smashed instead of growing, and Jupiter's gravity has been flinging pieces out of the belt ever since. That pattern holds for the whole solar system: almost all the mass outside the Sun is in the planets. The small bodies are numerous but light.

Did you know? The Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune is lightweight too. NASA estimates its total mass at no more than about 10% of Earth's.

7.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 1

Time to test what you've learned about asteroids. Why didn't the asteroid belt build a planet?

Is it A) Jupiter's tugs made the pieces smash, not stick, B) it was too hot there for rock to form, C) the Sun's gravity pulled the pieces in, or D) a planet formed there, then exploded? Look back at Slides 4 and 6, pick one, and be ready to explain why the other three don't work.

8.text:
Anatomy of a Comet

A comet is an icy leftover that grows a glowing coma and, usually, two tails near the Sun. Comets date back about 4.6 billion years and are made mostly of ice coated with dark, carbon-rich material, which is why NASA calls them "dirty snowballs."

Start at the center. The nucleus is a frozen chunk of ice and dust, a few km wide. Far from the Sun, that's all a comet is. As it gets close, sunlight warms the ice and it turns to gas. That builds a coma, a cloud of gas and dust around the nucleus that can stretch hundreds of thousands of kilometers. Then sunlight and the solar wind shove that gas and dust away into tails. An active comet near the Sun usually shows two: a straight, bluish ion tail and a curved, white dust tail. Nothing is on fire. It's all ice turning to gas.

We've visited comets up close. NASA's Deep Impact fired an impactor into comet Tempel 1 in 2005, and Stardust brought comet dust back to Earth in 2006. ESA's Rosetta became the first spacecraft to orbit a comet when it reached comet 67P on 6 August 2014, and its lander Philae touched down that November. The mission ended on 30 September 2016.

Did you know? Rosetta found that comet 67P's water is quite different from Earth's water. Comets may have brought water to the early Earth, but not every comet's water matches ours.

9.text:
A Comet Would Float

Try this one on. If you could drop a comet nucleus into a giant bathtub, it would float!

A comet nucleus is about 600 kg per cubic meter. Water is 1,000, and rock is about 3,000. A comet is so fluffy and porous, full of tiny empty spaces, that it's less dense than water. Think of a scoop of dry oatmeal, and forget the solid ice cube.

Did you know? A comet nucleus is less dense than plain ice, too, because of all that empty pore space.

10.text:
Tails Point Away From the Sun

Here's where most people get comets wrong. A comet's tail is not exhaust streaming out behind it like smoke from a car. Sunlight and the solar wind push the gas and dust away from the Sun, so both tails always point away from the Sun, wherever the comet is in its orbit.

The ion tail is charged gas blown straight away from the Sun by the solar wind, which flows outward at about 400 km per second. The dust tail is white and curves gently, in a slightly different direction. Watch how the tails change around the orbit. Closest to the Sun, the ices heat up the most and the tails get longest. Heading back out, the tail goes first, leading the comet. Far from the Sun, the nucleus freezes again: no coma, no tail.

Comets also wear out. NASA estimates a comet the size of Halley loses about 1 to 3 m of its surface each orbit. An average comet that keeps coming back lasts about 1,000 trips around the Sun.

Did you know? You can model this with a flashlight and a fan: no matter which way the "comet" moves, the "wind" from the Sun keeps blowing its tail the same way.

11.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 2

Picture a comet that just swung around the Sun and is now heading away from it. Where does its ion tail point?

Is it A) away from the Sun, so ahead of the comet, B) behind the comet, along its path, C) toward the Sun, or D) nowhere, because tails form only on the way in? Think back to what pushes the tail on Slide 10. Choose your answer and sketch it to back it up.

12.text:
The Kuiper Belt

The Kuiper Belt is a thick donut of icy bodies beyond Neptune, about 30 to 50 AU from the Sun. Its inner edge starts at Neptune's orbit, at 30 AU, and the main belt ends near 50 AU. A scattered disk of objects on stretched, tilted orbits continues out to nearly 1,000 AU.

There may be millions of icy objects out there, including hundreds of thousands larger than 100 km, made of rock, water ice and frozen stuff like ammonia and methane. Pluto, found in 1930, was the first Kuiper Belt object discovered. In 2019, NASA's New Horizons flew past one called Arrokoth, the most distant object ever explored up close. Like the asteroid belt, this region is a pile of leftovers that might have formed a planet if a giant planet, this time Neptune, hadn't stirred it up.

This is also where short-period comets are made. Follow the slide's steps: icy bodies collide, and Neptune nudges a piece inward. Then Jupiter corrals it into a short loop of 20 years or less. That's a Jupiter-family comet. Comet 67P, which Rosetta visited, is one of them.

Did you know? The Kuiper Belt is named for Gerard Kuiper, who wrote about it in 1951, but Kenneth Edgeworth had already speculated about it in the 1940s.

13.text:
The Oort Cloud

Now zoom way, way out. In 1950 the Dutch astronomer Jan Oort proposed that some comets come from a giant shell of icy bodies surrounding the whole solar system. Today we call it the Oort Cloud. On this drawing, the Sun, the planets and the Kuiper Belt are just the dot in the middle.

The inner edge of the cloud is thought to sit 2,000 to 5,000 AU from the Sun, and the outer edge somewhere between 10,000 and 100,000 AU. Let's check that big number. 100,000 AU times 1.496 × 108 km per AU is about 1.5 × 1013 km. Divide by 9.46 × 1012 km per light-year and you get about 1.6 light-years. That's a possible outer edge perhaps a quarter to halfway to the next star!

Nobody has ever seen the Oort Cloud directly. Its objects are too small and too far away. We know it's there from comet orbits: long-period comets fall in from every direction, not just along the flat plane of the planets. That's why Oort pictured a thick bubble instead of a flat belt. It may hold hundreds of billions to trillions of icy bodies, flung out there by the giant planets, mostly Jupiter, after the planets formed.

Did you know? Some Oort Cloud comets take up to 30 million years to orbit the Sun once. Even sunlight needs 10 to 28 days just to reach the cloud's inner edge.

14.text:
Visitors From Other Stars

Comets from the Oort Cloud still belong to our Sun. But a few objects don't. They formed around other stars, got thrown out of their home systems, drifted between the stars, and happened to pass through ours. Only 3 have been seen so far.

1I/'Oumuamua was found in October 2017 by the Pan-STARRS1 telescope in Hawaii. It was the first confirmed object from another star. 2I/Borisov was found in August 2019 by amateur astronomer Gennady Borisov, and it was the first confirmed interstellar comet. 3I/ATLAS was reported in July 2025 by the ATLAS survey telescope in Chile.

The "I" in each name means interstellar: from between the stars. The IAU created that letter in November 2017, and the numbers count up in order of discovery: 1I, 2I, 3I.

Did you know? Some people wonder if these visitors are alien spacecraft. All three behave like natural rocks or comets, and no evidence points to technology.

15.text:
How We Know They're Interstellar

Everything that orbits the Sun follows an ellipse, a closed loop, and keeps coming back. Astronomers measure how stretched an orbit is with a number called eccentricity, or e. A circle has e = 0. Ellipses, like the orbits of planets and comets, have e from 0 to 1. More than 1, and the path is a hyperbola: an open path, not a closed loop. The object swings past the Sun once and leaves forever.

Here are the measured values from NASA JPL. 1I/'Oumuamua: e = 1.20. 2I/Borisov: e = 3.36. 3I/ATLAS: e = 6.14. All three are above 1. Run each path backward in time, and it starts outside the solar system.

Speed tells the same story. 'Oumuamua moved about 26 km/s in deep space and about 87 km/s near the Sun. That's too fast for the Sun to hold.

Did you know? A very stretched orbit doesn't automatically mean "interstellar." Oort Cloud comets have extremely stretched orbits, but their e is still below 1.

16.text:
What Each Visitor Taught Us

Three visitors, three surprises. First, 'Oumuamua: a long, reddish rock with no tail, yet it sped up a little as it left, the way a comet might. NASA describes it as up to about 400 m long and perhaps 10 times longer than it is wide. Why it sped up is still debated, but scientists have proposed natural causes, like gas escaping from ice.

Second, Borisov looked like a normal comet, with a fuzzy coma just like comets from our own solar system. The lesson: other stars make comets too. Third, 3I/ATLAS was watched by many NASA missions, which saw water, carbon dioxide and organic (carbon-based) molecules. Now we can measure what another star system's comet is made of.

Plenty is still unknown. NASA estimates one of these visitors passes by about once a year, unseen, because most are too faint to spot. That's an estimate, not a count, and new sky surveys should tell us how common they really are.

17.text:
Check for Understanding: Do the Math

Your turn to be the astronomer. Use Kepler's third law, P2 = a3, to find how often Halley's Comet returns.

Here's your data. At its closest, Halley is 0.59 AU from the Sun. At its farthest, it is 35.25 AU away. The average distance is a = (closest + farthest) / 2.

Work it in three steps. 1. Find a, in AU. 2. Solve P2 = a3 for P, in years. 3. Sketch the orbit. Watch out for the classic traps: using the farthest distance instead of the average, and drawing a circle when the real shape is something else. Where does the Sun go in your sketch?

18.text:
What Makes a Planet?

On 24 August 2006, the International Astronomical Union (IAU), meeting in Prague, voted on a definition. A planet orbits the Sun, is nearly round, and has cleared its orbit. It has to pass all three tests.

Test (a): it orbits the Sun, not a planet. That rules out moons. Test (b): it's nearly round, because its own gravity pulled it into a ball. Small bodies stay lumpy. Test (c): it has cleared its orbit, with no crowd of bodies left in its lane.

That leaves eight planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Pluto passes (a) and (b) but fails (c), since other objects cross its path. What triggered the vote? The 2005 discovery of Eris, a world about Pluto's size. Astronomers had to choose between adding more planets or defining the word.

Did you know? There's no size rule in the definition. Pluto wasn't kicked out for being too small; it fails the "cleared its orbit" test.

19.text:
Meet the Dwarf Planets

A dwarf planet is round and orbits the Sun, but has not cleared its orbit, and is not a moon. The IAU named the first ones in 2006, and this drawing shows three of them to scale next to our Moon.

Ceres is 952 km wide and sits 2.8 AU from the Sun, in the asteroid belt. It was found in 1801 and called an asteroid for many years, and in 2015 it became the first dwarf planet visited by a spacecraft, NASA's Dawn. Pluto is 2,377 km wide at 39 AU, in the Kuiper Belt. It has five moons and mountains of water ice, and New Horizons flew past it on 14 July 2015. Eris is 2,326 km wide at 68 AU, in the scattered disk. It's slightly smaller than Pluto but has a bit more mass, and it takes 557 years to orbit the Sun.

Now compare them with our Moon, at 3,475 km wide. All three dwarf planets are smaller than the Moon! And there are more than three: the IAU recognizes five, including Haumea and Makemake out in the Kuiper Belt.

Did you know? Ceres may be as much as 25% water, and it has large salt deposits on its surface.

20.text:
Pluto Dances With Neptune

Pluto's orbit crosses Neptune's, so why don't they ever crash? They're locked in a 3 : 2 rhythm. Neptune orbits the Sun 3 times while Pluto orbits 2 times. The pattern repeats, so Neptune is never nearby when Pluto crosses its path. Pluto never comes close to Neptune. It actually gets closer to Uranus!

Neptune's orbit sits at 30 AU. Pluto's orbit is stretched and tilted, ranging from 30 to 49 AU. From 1979 to 1999, Pluto was actually closer to the Sun than Neptune was.

This is the same resonance idea from the Kirkwood gaps on Slide 4, but with a twist. In the asteroid belt, resonance clears lanes. Here, it protects Pluto. Check it with Kepler's third law: Pluto's 248-year orbit gives an average distance of about 39.5 AU, and two Pluto orbits (496 years) take as long as three Neptune orbits, so Neptune needs about 165 years per lap.

Did you know? So many Kuiper Belt objects share Pluto's 3:2 rhythm that astronomers have a name for them: plutinos.

21.text:
Pluto Is Not Dead

Scientists expected Pluto to be cold and dead, a frozen, cratered ball. New Horizons found something much stranger.

There's a huge plain of nitrogen ice called Sputnik Planitia with no craters at all, which means that surface is younger than about 10 million years. There are mountains made of water ice. There are faults and cracks, and a thin nitrogen atmosphere. Only Sputnik Planitia is crater-free, though, not the whole planet.

Could there be an ocean below? Maybe. Some scientists think the cracks formed as a hidden ocean froze, but that's a hypothesis, not a fact yet. And what keeps Pluto's insides warm enough for all this activity? Nobody knows.

22.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 4

Put the IAU rules from Slide 18 to work. Sort each card into one of three groups: PLANET, DWARF PLANET, or SMALL SOLAR SYSTEM BODY.

Your cards are A) Earth, B) Ceres, C) Halley's Comet, and D) Eris. For each one, run through the three tests: does it orbit the Sun, is it round, and has it cleared its orbit? Be careful with the ones you might have learned under a different label in an earlier grade.

23.text:
Meteoroid, Meteor or Meteorite?

Same object, three names, depending on where it is. A meteoroid is a space rock, still in space, anywhere from a dust grain up to a small asteroid. When it slams into the atmosphere at high speed and burns up, the streak of light is a meteor, a "shooting star." If a piece makes it all the way down, the piece on the ground is a meteorite.

Most of these rocks never make it. Most are sand- to pea-size and burn up high in the air. Still, NASA estimates about 44,000 kg of meteoritic material falls on Earth every day. Meteorites that survive often wear a shiny, melted skin called a fusion crust, from their fiery trip down.

There are three main types of meteorites: irons, stones and stony-irons. More than 50,000 have been found, and 99.8% come from asteroids, with the rest from Mars and the Moon. Deserts, including icy Antarctica, are the best hunting grounds.

Did you know? A meteor brighter than Venus gets a special name: a fireball.

24.text:
Meteor Showers

On a clear night you can usually spot a few meteors an hour. A meteor shower is much more: it's Earth plowing through a comet's trail of dust. Earth reaches the same spot in its orbit at the same time each year, so showers come back on about the same dates.

The famous one is the Perseids. Comet Swift-Tuttle left a dust trail along its orbit, and Earth crosses it each August. Every Perseid is a tiny piece of that comet, which takes 133 years to orbit the Sun. At the peak, around August 12 to 13, you might see up to about 100 meteors an hour under perfect skies.

During a shower, meteors seem to fly out of one spot in the sky. Showers are named for the constellation near that spot, so the Perseids seem to come out of Perseus. They don't actually come from those stars, of course. It's like driving through snow: the flakes all seem to rush at you from one point ahead.

Did you know? Halley's Comet gives us two showers a year: the Orionids in late October and the Eta Aquariids in early May.

25.text:
Meteor Crater, Arizona

About 50,000 years ago, an iron-nickel meteorite blasted out this crater in the Arizona desert. Today Meteor Crater, also called Barringer Crater, is one of the best-preserved impact craters on Earth.

Check the numbers. The crater is about 1.2 km wide and 180 m deep, with a raised rim. The rock that made it? Only about 30 to 50 m wide. Most of it melted or vaporized on impact, so there's no giant meteorite buried at the bottom. On the drawing, the depth is stretched so you can see it.

Geologists studied the crater from the 1890s, but its impact origin wasn't confirmed until 1960. Scientists dated the impact by measuring rare atoms made in boulders thrown out by the blast, and several methods agree: about 49,000 to 50,000 years. The dry desert climate is why it still looks so fresh. There's been very little erosion.

Did you know? A crater is many times wider than the rock that made it. A 50 m space rock dug a hole more than a kilometer across.

26.text:
Not Like the Movies

In the movies, spaceships dodge and weave through asteroid fields packed with tumbling rocks. Real life is a lot more boring, at least for the pilot. Neighbor asteroids are hundreds of thousands to a million km apart. The belt is mostly empty!

That's why a real probe flies through without dodging anything. There are about 1 to 2 million asteroids 1 km or larger, but the space is so huge that they're spread very thin. All together, the belt's mass is only about 3% of the Moon's.

So a big hit on any one world is rare. But over millions of years, some leftovers still land, and that's where craters come from. Next: how a crater forms, step by step.

27.text:
Crater Step 1: Contact & Squeeze

Step 1 is contact. The rock hits and squeezes the ground beneath it, and a shock wave spreads out through the rock.

Here's the part that isn't obvious. An impact isn't like a pebble dropped into sand. The rock is moving so fast that its energy is dumped almost instantly, so the impact acts like an explosion. That's why nearly every crater is round, even when the rock comes in at a slant. Only very low hits, at less than about 15°, make oval craters.

28.text:
Crater Step 2: Dig Out

Step 2 is excavation. The shock wave throws rock up and out, digging a deep, steep bowl. Scientists call it the "transient" crater, because it's the biggest the hole ever gets, and it doesn't last.

All that thrown-out rock is called ejecta. Each chunk flies on its own arcing path and lands around the crater, building an ejecta blanket that reaches out about one crater radius. In the end, a crater is about 10 to 20 times wider than the rock that made it.

29.text:
Crater Step 3: Collapse

Step 3 is collapse. Rock isn't strong enough to hold up those steep walls, so they slump inward. Broken rock (called breccia) and melted rock fill in the bottom.

Now the crater is done. It's wider and shallower than the bowl from Step 2, with a raised rim around the edge. That's the shape you see at Meteor Crater.

30.text:
Bigger Hit, Different Shape

Not every crater is a simple bowl. Size changes the shape. Small craters are bowls, with a raised rim and a layer of broken rock inside.

Bigger craters are "complex." The floor rebounds upward into a central peak, the floor flattens out, and the walls slump into stair-step terraces. The very biggest impacts make huge multi-ring basins, rings inside rings.

Where's the cutoff? On the Moon, simple craters are under about 15 to 20 km wide, and basins are about 300 km and up. On Earth, with its stronger gravity, the switch from simple to complex happens at only about 2 to 4 km.

31.text:
Chicxulub & the Dinosaurs

66 million years ago, an asteroid slammed into what is now Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, at the edge of the Gulf of Mexico. It left a crater about 180 km wide, now buried under younger rock. The impact set off the K-Pg mass extinction, the one that ended the age of the dinosaurs.

The clue was hiding in the rocks. Look at the layers on the slide: Cretaceous rock from before, Paleogene rock from after, and between them a thin, iridium-rich layer. Iridium is rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids. In 1980, Luis and Walter Alvarez, Frank Asaro and Helen Michel proposed that a giant impact caused the extinction. The crater itself was found in 1991. Scientists also found shocked quartz in that layer, grains that only a high-speed impact can make.

The blast caused shock waves, a heat pulse and tsunamis. Then dust and gas cut off sunlight, cooled the planet and acidified the oceans, and food chains collapsed from the plankton up. NASA estimates about three-quarters of plant and animal species died out, including all the non-bird dinosaurs. Most didn't die in the blast. They died in the hard years after.

Did you know? Estimates of Chicxulub's width range from about 150 to 200 km, so "about 180 km" is a good middle value.

32.text:
DART Moved an Asteroid

Can we protect Earth from a space rock? First you have to find them. NASA uses telescopes and radar to track near-Earth objects (NEOs), asteroids and comets that come within 1.3 AU of the Sun. An asteroid is "potentially hazardous" if it's about 140 m or larger and its orbit comes within about 7.5 million km of Earth's. That means "keep watching," not "it will hit." NASA says no known asteroid big enough to cause widespread damage is likely to hit Earth for at least the next 100 years.

Then you test whether you can push one. NASA's DART spacecraft crashed into Dimorphos, the small moonlet of the asteroid Didymos, on 26 September 2022, at about 6.1 km/s. Neither asteroid was ever a danger to Earth. Before the hit, Dimorphos took 11 h 55 min to orbit Didymos. After: 33 min shorter.

NASA only needed a 73-second change to call it a success, so DART beat the goal by more than 25 times. The debris blasted off the asteroid acted like rocket exhaust and added an extra push. It was the first time humans changed the motion of a space object on purpose.

Did you know? ESA's Hera spacecraft launched in October 2024 and is due to arrive at Didymos and Dimorphos in November 2026 to study DART's crater.

33.text:
Why Earth Hides Its Craters

Earth is a bigger target than the Moon, and both have been hit many, many times. So why does the Moon look like a pockmarked golf ball while Earth has only about 190 known craters? Because Earth erases them.

Erosion is weather, water and living things wearing the land, and old craters, away. Plate tectonics recycles the crust, forming new rock and destroying old rock. And lava and sediment bury craters; Chicxulub is hidden under younger sediment.

The Moon has none of that. There's no air, no weather, no erosion, and no tectonics for billions of years. A crater, once made, just stays.

Did you know? Footprint trails left by Apollo 14 astronauts in 1971 were still visible from orbit in 2011. Nothing on the Moon wipes them away.

34.text:
Indiana's Hidden Crater

You don't have to go to Arizona to find an impact site. Kentland, Indiana, in Newton County, sits on an old impact scar that doesn't look like a crater at all.

The site is deeply eroded, so the bowl is gone. How do we know a space rock hit here? Shatter cones: rock cracked into cone shapes by a powerful shock wave, like the one from an impact. They prove it.

35.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 5

Time for the last check. Why does the Moon show far more craters than Earth?

Is it A) Earth erases craters by erosion and tectonics, B) the Moon is hit far more often, C) Earth's air burns up every space rock, or D) Earth has never been hit by an asteroid? Think about Meteor Crater, Chicxulub and Kentland as you decide. Pick one and explain what's wrong with each of the others.

36.text:
Exit Ticket

You traveled from the asteroid belt to the Oort Cloud and back down to the ground. Show what you know with three questions.

First, name the parts of a comet and say which way its tails point. Second, use the IAU rules to explain why Ceres is a dwarf planet and not a planet. Third, meteoroid, meteor, meteorite: where is each one?

Then pull out the quick-write from Slide 1 about asteroids, comets and meteors. Would you change anything? Finish by rating yourself again on the "I can" list from Slide 2.

37.text:
One More Question

Here's a bonus. Put the three crater steps in order. What happens in each?

Think back to Slides 27 to 29: what happens first, what happens in the middle, and how the crater ends up. Write one sentence for each step.

The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards. Here's what they ask you to do, in plain words.

ES.2.2: describe the different kinds of objects in the solar system, including planets, moons, comets, asteroids and protoplanets. Know that planets have been found orbiting other stars, and some drift through space orbiting no star at all. Describe how our solar system is organized, including rocky and giant planets, asteroid belts and the Oort Cloud.

ES.2.4: use math to describe how planets, moons, comets and asteroids move, and explain that Kepler's laws come from Newton's law of gravity and his laws of motion. Your main task for this standard was the Halley's Comet math on Slide 17. The meteors, showers and craters in this deck are enrichment that sets up the Earth science decks on weathering, rock dating and plate motion.
